newsitem.title: FRANCE: Paris bourse braces for busy 1997 after good 1996.
newsitem.headline: Paris bourse braces for busy 1997 after good 1996.

text.p: The partial privatisation of France Telecom and the creation of private pension funds in France should enliven activity this year on the bourse, the chairman of French stockmarkets association SBF said on Tuesday.

As well as trying to drum up more listings, the SBF is preparing for the transition to trading in euros once a single European currency has been established in 1999, chairman Jean-Francois Theodore told a news conference.
Last year was kind to investors in French equities who were disappointed in previous years by the bourse's weak performance relative to other markets.
In 1996, the CAC-40 index rose 23.71 percent. Although it did not break its 1994 record, the rally was among the biggest in Europe.
Secondary share indices gained even more. The SBF 120 finished up 26.1 percent, the SBF 250 26.7 percent and the MIDCAC 35.7 percent.
The SBF also launched the small cap Nouveau Marche in 1996, which had 18 listings by the end of the year for a total capitalisation of six billion francs.
The SBF is aiming this year for at least 61 new listings, up from 57 in 1996, with 30 of them targetted for the Nouveau Marche, Theodore said.
He said he hoped to eventually raise the number of new listings to above 70 for a renewal rate of more than 10 percent.
The bourse's capitalisation last year increased to 3,072 billion francs, up from 2,446 billion in 1995 and 2,412 billion in the previous year.
"I'm hoping for a good year (in 1997). Interest rates should stay low, private pension funds will be established and we're hoping for privatisations including France Telecom," Theodore said.
The government is expected to place about 20 percent of the state-owned telecommunications group on the market in the spring for an estimated at 25 billion francs.

This compares with total 1996 offerings and capital increases of 67 billion francs, a figure that Theodore characterised as "very insufficient" in light of the estimated 800 billion francs saved annually in France.
"We think we could do better this year," he said. "We hope that the private pension funds, low interest rates, and the placement of France Telecom will lead to an increase."
Looking ahead, the SBF has begun planning for the "Big Bang" on January 4, 1999, when bourses in countries taking part in monetary union begin trading in the new currency.

Theodore said the SBF was in talks with financial newspapers, which are studying ways to prepare individual investors for the switch by listing stocks in both francs and euros during a transition period.
"For us, it's a very important job...It's not just a technical switch but it involves a major information campaign," he said. The SBF plans to unveil the campaign at mid-year.

Banks switching over their back-room operations face the biggest technical challenge. "For us, the essential challenge is the Big Bang. We close trading in francs on December 31 (1998) and resume trading on January 4 in euros," he said. "People know they won't be taking vacations that weekend."
Among the figures highlighting the bourse's 1996 performance, the SBF reported that the daily number of trades jumped to an average of 154,000 last month from 109,000 in December 1995.
The five most active shares on the primary market in 1996 were Elf-Aquitaine, Total, LVMH, Carrefour and Generale des Eaux.
